paras: The threatened lynching of Jake Lewis and others at Graball, Texas, was a reported threat by local citizens in January 1882 against Black men arrested for the murder and beheading of Jordan Thompson, a Black man. No lynching took place; Lewis pleaded guilty, was held in jail, and in April was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to twenty years. The threat is known only from a telegraphic brief, while the local paper described an excited crowd held back from the courthouse by guards.

In early January 1882 the body of Jordan Thompson, described as 'colored', was found near Graball with the head cut off. According to a paragraph credited to the Brenham Banner, he had been killed 'last Thursday night', and his body was found in a ravine covered with brush and logs. The Banner later reported that he was killed with a club, his head was then nearly severed with an axe, and the corpse was buried in a gully some distance away.

Jack Lewis, Adam Felder, Andrew Watts and Thompson's wife Lizzie were arrested and turned over to constable A. D. Gee, and a jury of inquest at Graball found that Thompson had been murdered by the three men. Deputy sheriff Spencer and a posse took the prisoners to Washington, where Justice G. W. Brooks held a preliminary examination. Lewis pleaded guilty against the justice's caution, saying he did not want others to suffer for his act, and the rest were released for lack of evidence.

During the examination the excitement was very high, and the constable placed guards at the courthouse doors to keep the crowd back. That Monday night, three masked men tried to rescue Lewis from his guard at Washington, but Gee was warned in time; the guard thought the men were negroes. A wire special datelined Courtney, Texas, reported that three negroes had been arrested near 'Grabele', had confessed, and that 'the citizens threaten lynching.' Because of high water, Gee brought Lewis by rail to Brenham and turned him over to the sheriff at the county jail.

At the April 1882 term of the district court, a jury found Jacob Lewis guilty of manslaughter after about half an hour, and he was sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary without appeal. His earlier confession was not admitted because of 'some informality'. Lizzie Thompson was acquitted by order of the court for want of evidence, the county attorney dismissed the charge against Andrew Watts, and Adam Felder's case was continued. No later report of Felder's case was found.

Outside Texas, the case appeared as one line among the 'Telegraphic Items' of The Silver State in Unionville, Nevada, which garbled the place name, credited all the prisoners with a confession, and closed on the lynching threat. The Brenham Weekly Banner, the local paper, headed its account 'The Graball Murder', named the officials and followed the case through the courts, calling the killing 'a brutal one' without mentioning lynching. The Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman reprinted a short version from the Banner that stressed the suspicion against the victim's wife.

The wire said three men were arrested and all confessed, while the Banner reported four arrests and a guilty plea from Lewis alone; the Banner's account, which names the officials and the proceedings, is the more detailed. The papers also differ on when the body was found: 'last Sunday' in the Banner's first report and 'on Saturday' in the Statesman's paragraph.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Jake Lewis and others at Graball, Texas
bases: The only report of mob action is a wire brief saying 'The citizens threaten lynching' against the arrested men (A2); the local paper reports a crowd held back from the courthouse by guards but no lynching attempt (A1), so this is at most a threatened lynching.

No one was killed by a mob: the threat reported in A2 was not carried out, and the accused Jake Lewis was jailed, tried and sentenced to twenty years for manslaughter (A1, A4). The killing of Jordan Thompson was a homicide charged to individuals, not a mob.

The murder, arrests and court case are reported independently by the Brenham Banner and a Texas wire special (A1, A2, A4), but the lynching threat appears only in the wire brief (A2), and the local account describes only an excited crowd kept back by guards (A1).

accounts.label: Texas wire special ('Courtney')
accounts.gist: Three negroes arrested near 'Grabele' for murdering a negro named Jordan confessed; the body was beheaded and mutilated, and 'the citizens threaten lynching.'

accounts.label: Local paper (Brenham Banner)
accounts.gist: Four people were arrested and examined; only Jake Lewis pleaded guilty and the rest were released. The courthouse crowd was excited and kept back by guards, and three masked men, thought by the guard to be negroes, tried to rescue Lewis.

framing.detail: A Nevada paper ran the case as one line among 'Telegraphic Items', leading with the arrest of 'three negroes' and ending 'The citizens threaten lynching.'
The Brenham Banner headed its account 'The Graball Murder' and followed the case through inquest, examination and trial, describing the crime as 'a brutal one' without mentioning lynching.
The Austin Statesman ran a short paragraph credited to the Banner about the murder and the suspicion against the victim's wife.
